questions.prompt: Compare serial queues and concurrent queues in Grand Central Dispatch. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that serial queues execute tasks one at a time in FIFO order.
Explains that concurrent queues start tasks in FIFO order but execute multiple tasks simultaneously.
Notes that completion order on concurrent queues depends on task duration.

questions.modelAnswer: A serial queue executes tasks one by one in strict First-In-First-Out order, waiting for each task to complete before starting the next. A concurrent queue starts tasks in FIFO order but runs them simultaneously across multiple worker threads. On concurrent queues, completion order is non-deterministic and depends on the duration of each task.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between `async` and `sync` dispatch methods in Grand Central Dispatch. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that async schedules the task and returns immediately to the caller without waiting.
Explains that sync blocks the calling thread until the submitted closure finishes execution.
Clarifies that async/sync controls caller waiting, not queue serialization.

questions.modelAnswer: The `async` method schedules a closure on a dispatch queue and returns immediately, allowing the calling code to continue running. In contrast, `sync` pauses the calling thread until the submitted closure completes its execution. These methods determine whether the calling thread waits, regardless of whether the queue is serial or concurrent.

questions.prompt: What are Quality of Service (QoS) classes in GCD, and what do they determine? Provide two examples. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that QoS classes specify the priority and urgency of work submitted to dispatch queues.
Identifies at least two specific QoS classes (e.g., userInteractive, userInitiated, utility, or background).
Notes that the system uses QoS to balance CPU scheduling and energy consumption.

questions.modelAnswer: Quality of Service (QoS) classes indicate the priority of tasks submitted to dispatch queues. They help the system balance CPU resources and battery power efficiently. For example, `userInteractive` provides highest priority, while `background` runs low-priority maintenance.

questions.prompt: What causes a deadlock when calling `queue.sync` from within the same serial queue? Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that calling sync pauses the currently executing task until the inner task completes.
Explains that the inner task cannot start because the serial queue is blocked by the waiting task.
Concludes that both tasks wait for each other indefinitely, causing a freeze.

questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock occurs because calling `queue.sync` pauses the active task until the new inner block finishes running. However, because the serial queue executes only one task at a time, the inner block cannot start until the active task finishes. Both tasks end up waiting for each other indefinitely, freezing the thread permanently.

questions.prompt: Why has Swift Concurrency (async/await and actors) replaced Grand Central Dispatch for modern Swift development? Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift Concurrency eliminates thread explosion using a cooperative thread pool matching CPU core count.
Mentions compile-time data race safety enforced through actors and Sendable checks.
Notes cleaner asynchronous syntax without deeply nested closure callbacks.

questions.modelAnswer: Swift Concurrency replaces GCD because it eliminates thread explosion by using a cooperative thread pool that matches the physical CPU core count. When an async task suspends, it yields its thread rather than blocking it. Furthermore, Swift 6 actors and strict concurrency checks provide compile-time protection against data races, whereas GCD lacks compile-time safety.
